Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) Technology Applied Materials Inc (NASDAQ:AMAT) 369.40 USD -12.520 3.278% Last Updated at: 2026-11-04T21:09:00Z told the market recently that it has entered an accelerated share acquisition agreement for shares of BE Semiconductor Industries, the Dutch maker of chip assembly equipment better known as Besi. Combined with the shares the American toolmaker already owns, the new agreement is meant to bring its position to roughly one fifth of Besi's outstanding common stock. The filing is short on numbers. It does not state a price, a US currency amount or the count of shares involved, and it does not name the bank on the other side of the accelerated arrangement.

What it does state is the destination, a notable share of Besi, together with the one gating item: delivery of the shares depends on the waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act ending or being terminated. No closing date was given. The move lands in a busy stretch for the company. Over the past several weeks Applied Materials has opened a very large research hub in Silicon Valley, signed collaboration news with several chipmakers, and set a date for its quarterly release later this month. The Besi step adds a capital allocation decision to that run of announcements, and it points at one of the more closely watched corners of the chip supply chain, advanced packaging.

The company said it will raise its position in Besi through an accelerated share acquisition agreement. In plain terms, an accelerated share acquisition is a contract under which an acquirer agrees to take a block of stock from a financial counterparty on a fast timetable, with the final settlement details worked out over a later averaging period. The company did not disclose the counterparty or the size of the block. What the release does fix is the end state.

sum: Applied Materials stock traded at 336.98 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 13:31 CET on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, 0.70 percent below the Xetra close of Tuesday, November 3. Investors can follow the real-time quote of Applied Materials stock.

The immediate market debate is no longer limited to demand for semiconductor equipment. It now centers on whether Applied Materials can convert strong artificial-intelligence-related demand into durable revenue and profit growth while customers, exchange-traded funds and investors reassess the sector's valuation.

In an analysis published on November 3, Simply Wall St said adjusted earnings per share had grown 41 percent and DRAM revenue 52 percent. The analysis contrasted those operating gains with sector-wide exchange-traded fund selling and a sharp October pullback in the stock.

That contrast is central to the current investment case. The analysis said the longer-term thesis depends on AI demand, higher-value packaging, services and Applied Materials' EPIC ecosystem continuing to attract customer spending. Near-term performance, however, remains exposed to capital-allocation decisions in leading-edge logic, DRAM and advanced packaging.

Applied Materials' plan to lift its holding in BE Semiconductor Industries to about 20 percent from roughly 9 percent adds another dimension. The companies already cooperate on hybrid bonding, a technology used to connect chips more densely for applications including high-bandwidth memory.

The larger investment gives Applied Materials a closer link to advanced-packaging economics, but it also raises execution risk. If customers delay hybrid-bonding deployments or pricing weakens, the strategic benefit could take longer to appear. The analysis also pointed to heavy investment in capacity, facilities and staff as a risk to free cash flow and margin expansion.

Analyst projections cited by Simply Wall St call for revenue growth of 23.8 percent a year over three years, with profit margins rising from 30.1 percent to 33.5 percent. Those estimates imply a demanding operating path: stronger AI-related demand must coexist with continued investment and a more selective semiconductor spending environment.

Is Applied Materials Still The Company You Bought?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Many investors bought Applied Materials (AMAT) for two reasons: the wide margins on its chip-making tools, and a steady flow of cash returned to shareholders through buybacks and dividends. On October 12, two months after reporting record quarterly revenue, the company unveiled a $5 billion research center for chip equipment. Management had said in August that the first research tool would move into the center the following week. Does a company spending on that scale still pay you back the way it used to?
Partly: Applied Materials Now Reinvests Far More Than Before

Applied Materials continues to sell chip-making machines through Semiconductor Systems and service work through Applied Global Services, but the company now redirects a much larger share of its revenue back into buildings and equipment. Over the last twelve months, capital spending reached about 9% of revenue, compared with a typical level of 2.8% from October 2011 to July 2025.

The latest quarter reflects the same shift. Capital spending in fiscal Q3 2026 alone reached $707 million, or nearly 8% of revenue for the period. While that remains far above the typical level, it is down from nearly 12% in fiscal Q4 2025.

Applied Materials is spending more because it is adding capacity on the strength of longer-term demand signals from its customers, management said on the August 13, 2026 call. Management added that the capital spending includes equipment for the new research center alongside other investments, and that the company's largest customers are now providing longer-term commitments and rolling forecasts.

The company opened a new manufacturing center in Singapore during fiscal Q3 2026, and management said that Applied Materials has nearly doubled its manufacturing space over the past several years. By 2028, it plans to have the capacity to double its quarterly output of systems from current levels.

“We’re not going to give a specific WFE forecast today,” Applied Materials (AMAT) CEO Gary Dickerson told investors at the company’s SEMICON West breakfast on Oct. 13, 2026. He followed it with “tremendous confidence” that computing demand would keep growing. Even so, reports from BigGo and Dow Jones tied the stock’s extra decline to the missing number. Shares closed down 6.69% at $464.24 that day and fell to $430.01 by Oct. 15, an eighth straight losing session.

The sector was already sliding. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had dropped for six sessions by Oct. 13, and memory stocks fell hard that day after a report on China’s ChangXin Memory. Lam Research (LRCX), KLA (KLAC) and ASML (ASML) lost 2.6% to 3.5%, about half of Applied’s decline or less.

The breakfast did deliver targets, laid out in Applied’s investor relations materials: a 54% non-GAAP gross margin and a 40% non-GAAP operating margin by calendar 2030. CFO Brice Hill put the current gross margin at about 50%. TIKR’s fiscal 2026 consensus shows an EBIT margin of around 33%.

Hill then gave the bridge. “We’ll expect to get 4 additional points on the gross margin. And we will expect to achieve 200 to 300 basis points in operating leverage,” he said. He credited AI automation in corporate functions for the second part. The pieces add up: around 33%, plus 4 points, plus 2 to 3 points lands near 40%.
He expects about 100 basis points of gross margin gain a year, though not in a straight line. He also said Applied is raising prices, partly to cover costs such as fuel and rare earths.

Services may be the most overlooked target. Applied Global Services generated $6.385 billion in fiscal 2025, and Applied targets more than $12 billion by calendar 2030. Bernstein’s Stacy Rasgon asked why connected chambers rising from 37,000 to 90,000 only yields mid-teens growth. Hill answered that the installed base grows 5% to 10% a year, and new products supply the rest.

sum: Applied Materials (AMAT-US), a leading semiconductor equipment maker, unveiled specific targets for significantly improved profitability and market share expansion by 2030 at its investor day, but did not provide an overall revenue forecast or a clear estimate of wafer fab equipment (WFE) market growth. This left investors—who had hoped the AI investment boom would continue driving equipment demand—deeply disappointed. The stock tumbled 6.69% on the 13th to close at $464.24 (approximately NT$15,000), its lowest close since September 21, marking the steepest single-day decline among the 30 components of the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index.

Applied Materials released its long-term operating outlook at the 2026 SEMICON West investor breakfast on the 13th. The company expects that as global AI infrastructure expansion accelerates, wafer fab equipment demand will surge, with overall equipment spending growth through 2030 outpacing the previous decade. On long-term financial targets, the company projects non-GAAP gross margin of approximately 54% and non-GAAP operating margin of approximately 40% by 2030, while committing to return 80% to 100% of free cash flow to shareholders.

Notably, Applied Materials posted adjusted gross margin of 48.8% and adjusted operating margin of 30.2% in 2025. In other words, if the company achieves its 2030 financial targets, these two metrics would improve by roughly 5 percentage points and 10 percentage points respectively—a substantial enhancement. Additionally, the company aims to expand its wafer fab equipment market share by more than 2 percentage points between 2025 and 2030.

CEO Gary Dickerson noted that AI computing technology continues to evolve from generative AI to agentic AI and physical AI, dramatically expanding demand for silicon and directly driving wafer fab equipment investment beyond previous industry growth momentum. He expects that between 2025 and 2030, advanced foundry and logic, DRAM, and advanced packaging will contribute approximately 75% of overall wafer fab equipment growth, and Applied Materials holds the leading position in process equipment across all three segments.

sum: Applied Materials (AMAT) sold a record $7 billion of chipmaking tools in fiscal Q3 2026. That was about 77% of its $9.1 billion in revenue for the quarter. When you own the stock, you mostly own those tool sales. A record that large is easy to read as the new normal. So what might Applied Materials investors be overlooking about those tool sales?

Investors can overlook how much Applied Materials’ tool sales depend on space its customers control. Chipmakers run these tools inside clean rooms, the sealed, dust-free floors of a chip factory. Management said in the fiscal Q3 2026 call that clean room availability will determine what the industry can ship in 2027.
Take a made-up chipmaker whose clean room is already full of tools. It cannot buy another tool until it builds more space or frees some up.

In 2026, customers found new ways around those space limits, management said. As a result, they sharply raised their demand for tool deliveries. Sales of tools for DRAM, a type of memory chip, grew 52% from a year earlier to a record. That growth includes packaging tools for high-bandwidth memory. You can see how quickly that demand came in Applied Materials’ own sales.

Applied Materials’ sales turned around within a year. In the oldest of the last four quarters, revenue was 3.5% lower than a year earlier. By fiscal Q3 2026, revenue was 24.8% higher than a year earlier. Tool sales grew faster still, rising 27% from a year earlier.

Revenue fell from a year earlier in two of those four quarters, so this growth is recent. Even so, Applied Materials is building for more demand. Management said the company can double its quarterly tool output from current levels by 2028. Management also said that is a capacity plan, not a revenue forecast for 2028.

Management said Applied Materials’ capital spending, the money it puts into buildings and equipment, will stay higher than normal in 2027. That spending will still fall as a share of revenue. For fiscal Q4 2026, the company expects tool sales of around $7.9 billion, above the fiscal Q3 record. The company gave no figure for fiscal Q1 2027, though management said it expects that quarter to grow from fiscal Q4. Management has given no growth figure for 2027, yet the price you pay likely assumes the pace will last.

items.t: “Most important company you’ve never heard of”
sum: "The New York Times" veteran commentator Thomas Friedman once wrote, "Applied Materials is one of the most important US companies you've probably never heard of." There is a good reason why not many people have heard of it - it is a boring company that manufactures machines for testing microchips used in cloud servers, smartphones, and electric vehicles for defects. Its share price trod water on the New York Stock Exchange for years.
The company’s name was mentioned mainly in reports about organizational changes or layoffs. Its executives granted few interviews other than for launches of new products and kept a low profile.

In the early 2000s, Ofer Greenberger, 64, was known as the CEO of KLA-Tencor, a competitor of Applied Materials. He was appointed CEO of Applied Materials Israel in 2017, then left that job for a position as Group VP Strategic BD - M&A and Investments in Applied Materials' global headquarters.

Last year, Greenberger accepted an offer to resume his position at the head of Applied Materials' Israeli center. "I was on a different path in my life, so I took a timeout," he says in his first-ever interview to "Globes."

Greenberger: "I went sailing for a few months. The situation to which I agreed to return was a completely different one. The Israeli center is no longer merely a development center of a global company; it is an independent business unit. Besides technological depth, it also features business acumen, awareness of competitive advantage, and a strong desire to take advantage of the surges in the market."

Greenberger asserts that over the past five years, the Israeli division has tripled its global sales, boosted its profit margin, and enhanced its potential. "We're now exploiting the rises in the market to grow as powerfully as we can," he declares. "Friedman wrote that Applied Materials was one of the most important US companies you've never heard of. Today, I can say that its Israeli division, the PDC division (Process, Diagnostics, and Control) is a company no less important to the global economy that many people have never heard of."
The timing selected by Greenberger for his interview is no accident.

sum: After a historic run, the biggest threat to the chip-equipment giant isn’t a lack of demand but the immense difficulty of executing flawlessly when expectations are this high.

If you hold Applied Materials (AMAT) stock, you’ve been rewarded for believing in the AI-driven demand for semiconductors. The company is firing on all cylinders, and the stock sits at its 52-week high after a strong run. But when a stock has priced in this much good news, the risks shift. The risk is no longer that the story is wrong, but that it has to be perfectly right, and reality rarely cooperates.

The current valuation leaves no room for error. The stock’s price-to-sales multiple recently hit 19.0, more than double its prior 10-year high of 9.4. Its price-to-earnings multiple of 64.8 is also twice its decade peak. That’s the kind of valuation that looks past simple growth and demands a flawless multi-year execution of it. The biggest risks, then, are the two things most likely to disrupt that perfect narrative.

The first risk is that the company’s high profitability may not be sustainable. Applied Materials recently delivered its “highest gross margin in more than 25 years,” and its net margin of 29.3% is the highest in at least five years, sitting well above its 3-year average of 26.0%. This is a sign of significant strength, reflecting leadership in high-value AI markets.

But it’s also a vulnerability. Peak margins are, by definition, hard to sustain. They invite competition or customer pushback on pricing or can simply normalize as product cycles mature or input costs rise. If profitability reverts toward its historical average, it would directly pressure earnings. For a stock priced at these levels, even a small compression in margins could be enough to force a significant re-evaluation by the market, as the current price is heavily dependent on this best-in-class profitability continuing indefinitely.

The second major risk is operational. The demand for equipment for artificial intelligence is so strong that management now expects its “semiconductor equipment business will grow more than 30% this calendar year.” That’s a significant acceleration from the 3.3% annual growth seen over the last twelve months. The valuation is banking on the company delivering this.

On June 25, shares spiked to an intraday record of $669.22 and closed up 13.42% after the company unveiled six new chipmaking systems aimed at AI memory. The next day, June 26, the stock dropped 6.16% to close at $626.84. That round trip is the whole debate in two sessions.

The one question the market cannot yet answer: did the AI capex cycle justify this re-rating, or has the price run past the fundamentals it is built on?

The catalyst was specific. On June 25, Applied introduced a suite of tools built for what it calls the AI “memory wall,” meaning the point where data movement outpaces gains in bandwidth and efficiency. The portfolio targets DRAM (the memory that feeds servers and AI accelerators) and advanced packaging (the process of stacking and connecting chips into a single high-performance system).

Prabu Raja, president of Applied’s semiconductor products group, framed the stakes plainly: “Advanced packaging has become a primary driver of system-level performance, and the complexity of next-generation 3D architectures demands new levels of precision across every process step.” That matters because packaging is shifting from a back-end afterthought to a front-line bottleneck for AI chip output, and Applied sells the deposition, etch, and inspection tools that bottleneck runs through.

If you want to understand Applied Materials (AMAT), don’t think of it as just another technology company. Think of it as a key link in the global artificial intelligence race.
